title: Genetic Epidemiology and Gene–Environment Interactions in Fibrodysplasia Ossificans Progressiva: From ACVR1 Mutations to Trauma- and Inflammation-Triggered Heterotopic Ossification
content: Fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP) is an ultra-rare, debilitating genetic disorder characterized by the progressive and irreversible heterotopic ossification (HO) of soft connective tissues, ultimately leading to permanent loss of mobility. It is predominantly caused by a heterozygous single-nucleotide substitution (c.617G>A; p.R206H) in the ACVR1 gene. This causes the receptor to become aberrantly responsive to Activin A, thereby hyperactivating bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) signalling. Notably, disease progression is heavily driven by gene–environment interactions; environmental and inflammatory triggers, such as mechanical trauma, viral infections, and invasive medical procedures, frequently induce flare-ups that accelerate HO. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the genetic epidemiology of FOP and how the interplay between ACVR1 mutations and environmental stimuli coordinates the pathogenesis of trauma- and inflammation-induced HO. Finally, we highlight current management paradigms and emerging therapeutic strategies aimed at mitigating this devastating condition.
